root_cause_label: Fragile Global Motion Heuristic Misidentifies Jump Event
one_sentence_failure_summary: The agent applies a naive global frame-difference heuristic that identifies the largest motion spike (frame 109) and largest drop (frame 113) near the end of the video as takeoff/landing, ignoring the actual hurdle clearance event visible in the diagnostic data at earlier frames, and then interprets all diagnostic evidence as confirming its wrong conclusion.
t_err_evidence: Step 4 creates jump_analyzer.py using first-frame background subtraction compared globally across all pixels, then uses the first and last frames with motion > threshold as takeoff and landing respectively. This heuristic lacks domain knowledge about jump detection and will capture general runner presence rather than the specific takeoff/landing event.
t_commit_evidence: Step 25 implements the final wrong algorithm: picks takeoff as the frame with the largest positive difference >5000 and landing as the frame with the largest negative difference after takeoff. This deterministically selects frames 109 and 113 (as confirmed in step 26), and the agent has no further strategy changes planned to correct this.
t_surface_evidence: Step 26 outputs 'Analysis complete. Takeoff: 109, Landing: 113', producing a jump window of only 4 frames at the very end of the 119-frame video, inconsistent with a hurdle clearance event that typically spans more frames and occurs earlier in approach videos.
trigger_explanation: The agent lacks domain knowledge about computer vision techniques for sports action detection (optical flow, pose estimation, foot-contact detection, ROI-based analysis near the hurdle). Instead it applies a naive global background-subtraction approach which accumulates drift as the runner progresses through the frame, systematically biasing later frames to have higher motion values unrelated to the jump event.
forewarning_evidence: Step 11 shows 'Takeoff: 0, Landing: 118' which the agent recognizes as wrong in step 13 ('the takeoff frame is detected as 0, which is the first frame of the video... this detection is incorrect'). Steps 15-16 still produce the same wrong takeoff=0 result, demonstrating the heuristic is not fit for purpose. The diagnostic data in step 18 shows motion already at 1447 pixels in frame 0, suggesting the runner is already present in the first frame (background assumption violated), which is a clear warning sign.
